newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU seeks way out of technology trade impasse.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU seeks way out of technology trade impasse.

text.p: The European Union on Tuesday stepped up pressure on Washington to begin work an International Technology Agreement by softening its opposition to a semiconductor alliance between the Japan and United States.
Sources said the European Commission -- which negotiates EU trade policy -- was backing down from an ultimatum that insists on immediate EU inclusion in the chip alliance.

But in return, they said, the EU would insist that discriminatory aspects of the alliance are not applied until progress has been made on the ITA, a hoped for agreement on technology trade between the EU, United Statea and Japan.
EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan is said to have outlined this proposal on Tuesday in a delicately phrased letter to his U.S. counterpart Charlene Barshefsky.
The sources said the letter reiterates EU opposition to the semiconductor alliance and also takes the offensive in calling for Washington to make the next move in the ITA saga.
The Commission hopes swift progress on a wide-ranged ITA -- in which the EU would have a strong voice -- would offset what it sees as an unfair deals on specific products such as semiconductors.

The move comes just two days before a meeting of trade officials from the United States, Canada, Japan and the EU in Seattle, Washington, where they are to discuss strategy ahead of December's World Trade Organisation meeting in Singapore.
EU officials believe the Seattle meeting is the last chance for work to begin on an ITA before the WTO ministerial.
Brittan's letter is said to accuse the U.S. and Japanese semiconductor industries of holding the ITA hostage, but avoids direct criticism of governments.
Barshefsky last week accused to EU of backing down from its committment for an ITA, a charge Brittan has strongly refuted.

While seeking a way forward, the Commission is expected to launch its defence soon by suggesting U.S. trade negotiators may not have a mandate to agree product-specific cuts in tariffs and other barriers.
The Commission says it wants an ITA to cover wide range of technology products, but officials fear the U.S. is seeking to exclude certain items.

Industry analysts say Brittan has little choice but to call for a wide ITA, as this is the only way he can trade-off European tariffs on semiconductors against areas such as capacitors and photocopiers where European companies are more competitive.
Washington and Tokyo signed an agreement in July which gives their respective semiconductor industries responsibilty for monitoring foreign access to their markets.
The alliance guarantees American chip producers at least 19 percent of the Japanese market, although in practise U.S. producers have enjoyed a greater share.
EU chip producers have just one percent of Japan's market, while U.S. and Japanese chip makers have a 66 percent share of the 15-nation bloc's sales.
